summary:
SkyLens is a free web app that turns real infrared images from NASA’s SPHEREx mission into a journey through time. Built for the “Planet X and SPHEREx” challenge, it lets anyone enter an object name or RA/Dec, or open one of the five challenge targets, and live pulls every SPHEREx frame of that spot from NASA/IPAC’s IRSA archive, aligns them and plays them as a time-lapse that reveals what moves or changes.

SkyLens brings SPHEREx, WISE, Gaia, SIMBAD and JPL Horizons into one viewer. Users can blink surveys months or a decade apart, track real asteroids, read the 0.75–5 μm spectrum of any star and subtract images to find changes, which the community then classifies by vote. Photon, our AI guide, explains what is on screen in plain English or Spanish. On a phone, SkyLens becomes an infrared lens that guides you to the target in the real sky.

SPHEREx data is open but hard to use: today it takes IRSA, Aladin, WiseView and Python. SkyLens puts it all in one link, speeding up research and giving students and teachers a real entry point into space science.
details:
Overview

SkyLens is a free, bilingual sky viewer that turns NASA's SPHEREx all-sky surveys into a time-lapse anyone can explore, on desktop or on a phone. It puts real mission data and the methods astronomers use in one link, explained in plain words.

Live prototype: spherex-skylens.vercel.app

What it does and how it works

SkyLens is a sky viewer that queries many archives at once. Users choose a target: one of the challenge targets, a featured field such as the Orion Nebula or the Pleiades, or any object name or RA/Dec. The server then finds every SPHEREx observation of that spot through IRSA's TAP service, downloads the cutouts, reprojects them north-up with the FITS WCS and streams the results to the browser.

How SkyLens works, from a target name to real SPHEREx data on screen.

Main features

See through time

Scrub or blink between SPHEREx's all-sky surveys and watch what moves or changes.

Orion Nebula, three SPHEREx surveys played in sequence.

Find what changed

Sources that appeared or faded are flagged on a two-colour difference image, cross-matched with SIMBAD and checked across the six detectors. Cosmic rays, hot pixels and flagged pixels are filtered out in plain view. The detector is validated with injection-recovery tests.

Before, after and difference, with the community vote underneath.

Moving objects

Track any asteroid live with JPL Horizons, and measure stellar proper motion against Gaia DR3, SIMBAD, CatWISE2020 and 2MASS.

Tested on the challenge targets: for Barnard’s Star, Gaia predicts 10.25″ of motion between Aug 2025 and Aug 2026; SPHEREx measured 10.4″ ± 0.8″.

Asteroid (3) Juno crossing four SPHEREx frames taken 26 hours apart.

Spectra and colour

Read the 0.75–5 μm spectrum of any point, with water ice, CO₂ ice, PAH and hydrogen lines marked, and see the six bands combined into a true-data colour image.

The spectrum of one spot, explained in plain words.

The six bands combined into a colour image built from calibrated pixel values.

WISE ↔ SPHEREx

Blink the same field across a decade.

Photon / Fotón

An AI guide (Claude via the Anthropic API) that answers questions about what is on screen using the real data. It only answers about the sky and SkyLens, and says so when it cannot answer.

Photon, the guide, greeting a new user.

Citizen science

Users classify each candidate as a real change, a moving object or an image glitch. Votes are shared live as a community tally and can be exported as JSON.

Find Planet X

A game where a fictional distant planet is painted into two real frames with realistic parallax. Players blink and find it, the same task Backyard Worlds volunteers do.

Expert mode

Aperture photometry, spectral typing against standard cold dwarfs, Gaia tracking with propagated uncertainties, DS9-style image controls, and a link to the same field in Aladin Lite. Every photometry measurement comes with the Python (photutils) script to reproduce it on the original IRSA file.

Aperture photometry: flux in mJy, AB magnitude and signal-to-noise.

Image controls: limits, stretch, sensitivity and the dates compared.

Infrared lens (AR)

On a phone, GPS, compass and tilt place the SPHEREx view over the real sky. An arrow guides the user until the target is in the circle.

Following the arrow, then on target.

Built for the challenge
Choose the field of view (0.17°, 0.34° or 0.68°), open any target straight from a URL with its coordinates or embed it with a ready-made iframe, and live searches query IRSA directly, so new SPHEREx releases show up as soon as they are published.

Benefits and intended impact

SkyLens brings together, in a single free viewer, work that today means downloading FITS files from IRSA, opening them in Aladin, comparing dates in WiseView and writing Python to measure them. For researchers, it speeds up search and comparison work. For teachers and students, it is an entry point into space science with real mission data.

It is bilingual (English/Spanish) and designed with Latin American classrooms and outreach in mind. Through community classification, users don't just look at science: they help produce it.

Before: four tools. Now: one link, on desktop or phone.

Impact in Costa Rica

Costa Rica already has a growing space ecosystem. More than 40 companies are part of its aerospace cluster, the country launched its first satellite, Irazú, built with the TEC, and Orbital Space was born from TEC students. SkyLens wants to be the entry point to that ecosystem for students, teachers and anyone curious about space.

  • For classrooms: the app is bilingual (Spanish/English) and has a plain-language mode, so a high school or university class can explore real NASA data without installing software or writing code.
  • For universities: Costa Rican astronomy and engineering students can practise with the same data and methods used in research, at no cost.
  • For the community: anyone in the country can classify what they find and contribute to real science. Votes are handled in line with Costa Rica’s personal data protection law (Ley 8968).
  • For responsible technology: SkyLens follows the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2024–2027 (MICITT): its AI is ethical, safe and centred on people.

Next step: bring SkyLens to Costa Rican universities, classrooms and outreach programs, starting with the institutions that already lead the country’s space projects.

Access

SkyLens is free by design, because the value is in access to open data. Next, we will add more data sources to the same viewer.

Scan to open SkyLens: spherex-skylens.vercel.app

Tools and technologies

Next.js 16 (App Router), React 19, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS v4, with a dependency-free processing core in Node. Live API routes stream progress as NDJSON.

Data comes from IRSA (TAP and IBE), JPL Horizons, the ESA Gaia archive, SIMBAD/CDS, unWISE and NOIRLab Astro Data Lab. Firebase (anonymous sign-in, Firestore) stores community votes. The Anthropic SDK powers Photon, with the API key kept server-side and questions filtered and rate-limited. The app is hosted on Vercel.

Creativity

Instead of a static image viewer, SkyLens treats time as the main dimension. It turns SPHEREx's repeated all-sky surveys into a time-lapse, so change becomes visible. Several archives answer in one place, and a friendly guide explains the results.

The interface itself follows the instrument: accents take the colour of the band being viewed, and Photon changes colour with the wavelength. On a phone, the same data becomes an infrared lens pointed at the real sky.

Photon, the SkyLens mascot: a photon riding its own wave.

Factors we considered

  • Real data only: the only thing ever added to an image is the fake planet in the Planet X game, and the game says so.
  • Honest limits: when a target is too faint or saturates the detectors, the app says so instead of inventing a measurement.
  • Proper credit to every source and license.
  • Responsible AI: Photon only answers about the sky and SkyLens, uses the real data on screen, and says so when it cannot answer.
  • Accessibility: 44 px touch targets, good contrast, and a plain-language mode with expert mode on demand.
  • Mobile and desktop layouts.
  • A multidisciplinary team combining Systems, Industrial and Chemical Engineering, Cybersecurity and Law.
